why: Lines 1-2 are literally my week: hot pot, staying up late, mouth ulcer, mom saying 上火. I recognise myself straight away. Line 3, where a researcher says 上火 'has no clear definition', is a small slap, because I always took 上火 as a fact. Then line 5, 顺着这把火会一路找到砒霜, is the real hook. I have no idea how a mouth ulcer leads to arsenic, so I stay to find out.
first_moment_I_got_curious: Line 5 (砒霜). Line 3 made me look up from the screen, but line 5 is what stopped my thumb.
where_I_would_swipe_away: Lines 12-17: after the capsaicin/Nobel bit (which was cool), the sleep study, sore throat (viruses) and acne (pores and bacteria) start to feel like a list of medical facts. It's the 'textbook voice' moment. The arsenic promise from line 5 is the only thing keeping me here.

Lines 21-26: 五行 plus 黄帝内经 plus ancient Greek four humors plus yellow bile. This is my biggest swipe risk. I came for my ulcer and arsenic, and now it's a world-history lesson. 黄胆汁又热又干 means nothing to me. Line 26 (both sides were classifying the world) is a nice idea, but it lands after I've already half-left.

Lines 33-38: lots of numbers close together (55 patients, 32 patients, 16 survived), and then line 38 about English-paper citations. If I'm tired, this is where I scroll on without having seen the 99.2% payoff.
lines_I_did_not_understand: #3: 研究上火的学者. Who? A Western doctor? A TCM scholar? It changes how I hear the line. If it's a TCM researcher saying so, I'm far more surprised.
#6: 症状是真的，'上火'是它们的俗称. 'Them' is which symptoms? At this point only the ulcer has been mentioned, so '它们' (plural) comes slightly too early.
#15: 其中一个，活跃度涨了3倍多. One what? One person? One gene? One immune cell? I honestly can't tell. I guessed gene, but I wasn't sure.
#11: The finding is from 1997 and the Nobel is 2021? I had to stop and check whether I'd misread. A 24-year gap with no explanation feels like an error.
#27: 比'火'更珍贵的，是两千多年的观察. What observation exactly? It sounds deep but I can't point to the thing being observed. Feels like a slogan.
#32: 不再百病都试. 'No longer' means they used to try it on every disease? Nobody told me that, so this line assumes a step I never saw.
#36 vs #33: are the 32 patients part of the 55, or a new group? I lost track.
#37: Is 16 out of 32 (half) surviving 5 years good or bad? Line 35 says it used to kill in weeks, so I think it's good, but I had to work that out myself. The video didn't spell it out.
#38: 很久没被英文论文引用. Why should I care? Is this saying the West ignored Chinese doctors? It reads like a grievance with no payoff, and the next line moves on as if it never happened.
#39: 后来逐个去掉. Who did? The Harbin team? The Shanghai team?
#41: 弄清了它为什么有效. Then why IS it effective? The line says they figured it out and doesn't tell me. That feels like a tease that never pays off.
#42: 维甲酸. Never heard of it. Fine as a name, but I don't know if it's also some old remedy or a normal Western drug.

#45-46: 99.2% vs 92.6%. My first reaction was 'only about 7 points apart?' I didn't feel how big that is until I thought about it. The chemo group also did well, so the 'wow' is weaker than the video seems to think.
#51: 张亭栋、王振义. The first time any names appear, right at the end. I don't know which one is Harbin and which is Shanghai. They feel like a credits roll.
takeaway_in_my_words: 上火 isn't one real disease. It's an old everyday label that sticks one word on lots of different real problems: ulcers, sore throats, spicy-mouth burn, acne, each with its own cause. The ancients picked 火 because red, hot, rising things look like fire. Old folk knowledge can contain real gold (arsenic really does treat one kind of leukemia), but it only counts once someone tests it properly. So 'my mom is right' and 'my mom is wrong' are both too simple.
surprise_that_stuck: Arsenic (砒霜), the classic poison from TV dramas, is now the standard treatment for one deadly leukemia, and with it 99.2% of patients were still alive after 4+ years without chemo. Second place: chili doesn't really 'burn'. It flips the same nerve switch as heat above 43°C, and that won a Nobel Prize. I'd repeat both to friends.
title_I_would_click: 3. 从上火到砒霜. It's a curiosity gap I can't close myself: how do you get from a mouth ulcer to poison? It's short and a bit dangerous-sounding. Title 1 (上火，到底是什么火？) is clear but reads like a standard 科普 account I've seen a hundred times. Title 2 (妈说你上火了) is relatable, but I'd expect a family-comedy skit or a lecture.
title_that_misleads: Two risks. Title 3 (从上火到砒霜): a careless scroller, or my parents' generation, might read it as 'arsenic treats 上火' or 'food that causes 上火 is as bad as poison'. Neither is what the video says, and the first is actually dangerous (line 49's disclaimer helps, but it's buried in the middle). Title 2 (妈说你上火了) suggests the video is about proving mom wrong or making fun of her. The video is more balanced than that, so it sets up a fight the content doesn't pick.
what_I_would_comment: "砒霜那段直接给我看起鸡皮疙瘩，99.2%是认真的吗" and then maybe "所以我妈说我上火，到底算对还是不对啊". The second is a real question, because the ending tosses it back to me instead of answering.
who_I_would_send_this_to: My roommate who blames everything on 上火 and drinks 凉茶 constantly. Also a friend in medical school, half to show off and half to ask if the 99.2% is real. I would NOT post it in the family group or send it to my mom directly. Even though the video is fair, sending it reads as 'see, you're wrong', and that starts an argument. Maybe I'd send it to my mom if the title were 1, not 2.
did_anything_feel_like_it_was_mocking_or: Mocking: mostly no. Line 55 (溃疡是真的，'火'是古人的比喻) is respectful, and line 27 actually praises the ancients. The only edge is line 54 (下次妈再说'你上火了'). It sounds like it's handing me ammo to correct my mom, and the 'mom' framing at both ends gives it a slight 'young people know better' vibe. Preaching: yes, a little, at the end. Lines 56-57 (老祖宗的话，哪些该信？哪些又该先验证？) are a moral-of-the-story ending, like a school essay. Line 27 is also a slogan-like line. Line 28 (还差一步：验证) is fine because a real story follows it. Line 38 (English-paper citations) feels like a quiet nationalist jab that's never explained, so I can't tell whether I'm meant to feel proud or annoyed.

for_frames_only.what_this_says_in_5s: No frames were included in my input (subtitles and titles only), so I can't judge visuals.
